t: Largest Element After Merge Operations — Right-to-Left Accumulation
o: You may merge nums[i] into nums[i+1] whenever nums[i] <= nums[i+1], replacing the pair by their sum. In [2,3,7,9,3] the chain 2+3=5, 5+7=12, 12+9=21 builds the answer 21; the trailing 3 cannot join since 21 > 3. In [5,3,3] merging right-to-left gives 3+3=6 then 5+6=11. Observation: scanning from the right, maintain the best obtainable value of the segment to the right; the current element can be absorbed into it iff nums[i] <= that value, mirroring the merge rule. The final answer is the maximum over all segments, which the scan computes directly.
k: Process right to left keeping 'ans' = best value achievable from the suffix.
If nums[i] <= ans, nums[i] can merge into the suffix block, so ans += nums[i].
Otherwise nums[i] starts a new block: ans = nums[i].

a.n: Approach 1: Reverse Scan with Running Maximum Block
a.i: Claim: the maximum reachable value equals what the reverse greedy produces. Any final large element is a sum of a contiguous block nums[i..j] where merges cascade left-to-right; such a cascade is possible exactly when each prefix of the block satisfies the merge condition, which the reverse scan checks implicitly: nums[i] joins the block headed by the suffix optimum iff nums[i] <= suffix optimum.
s: Set ans = 0 and iterate i from n-1 down to 0.
If nums[i] <= ans, set ans += nums[i]; else ans = nums[i].

a.n: Approach 2: Stack Simulation Left to Right
a.i: Push elements onto a stack; whenever the top two satisfy stack[-2] <= stack[-1], merge them. This simulates the natural cascading merges and ends with a strictly decreasing stack whose maximum is the answer. It matches the reverse-scan result and is more concrete to explain.
s: For each x: push x; while stack has >= 2 elements and stack[-2] <= stack[-1], replace them by their sum.
Return the maximum of the stack.
a.t: O(n) amortized — each element is pushed and popped at most once.
a.sp: O(n) — the stack can hold up to n elements.

w: Prefer Approach 1 for its simplicity and O(1) space; use the stack version if the interviewer wants an explicit simulation. Beware 32-bit overflow: sums reach 1e5 * 1e6 = 1e11, so use 64-bit types. Sanity checks: single element (returns itself), strictly decreasing input (returns nums[0]), strictly increasing input (returns the total sum). Follow-up: minimum possible final array length, or the lexicographically largest achievable array.
